Darboux's Theorem

A derivative keeps the intermediate value property even when discontinuous. Watch a wildly oscillating derivative step on every level.

A derivative cannot jump across values. To get from one value to another it must pass through everything between. Even a discontinuous derivative obeys this rule.

For example, a 🌡️ thermometer sliding from −1° to 1° passes through every temperature between. A derivative likewise never jumps over an intermediate value.

Prove as a corollary of Darboux's theorem: no function can have the Heaviside step function HHH (000 for x<0x < 0x<0, 111 for x≥0x \geq 0x≥0) as its derivative.

F′=H,F′(−1)=0<12<1=F′(1) →Darboux ∃ ξ∈(−1,1): F′(ξ)=12∉{0,1} ⇒⇐F' = H,\quad F'(-1) = 0 < \tfrac12 < 1 = F'(1)\ \xrightarrow{\text{Darboux}}\ \exists\, \xi \in (-1,1):\ F'(\xi) = \tfrac12 \notin \{0,1\}\ \Rightarrow\LeftarrowF′=H,F′(−1)=0<21​<1=F′(1) Darboux​ ∃ξ∈(−1,1): F′(ξ)=21​∈/{0,1} ⇒⇐
Show proof

  1. Suppose some FFF, differentiable on all of R\mathbb{R}R, had HHH as its derivative.

    Take a=−1a = -1a=−1, b=1b = 1b=1: then F′(−1)=H(−1)=0F'(-1) = H(-1) = 0F′(−1)=H(−1)=0 and F′(1)=H(1)=1F'(1) = H(1) = 1F′(1)=H(1)=1.

    Since 0<12<10 < \frac{1}{2} < 10<21​<1, Darboux's theorem (problem 1) gives some ξ∈(−1,1)\xi \in (-1,1)ξ∈(−1,1) with F′(ξ)=12F'(\xi) = \frac{1}{2}F′(ξ)=21​.

  2. But HHH takes only the values 000 and 111, so F′(ξ)=H(ξ)=12F'(\xi) = H(\xi) = \frac{1}{2}F′(ξ)=H(ξ)=21​ is impossible — a contradiction. Hence no function has HHH as its derivative.

  3. In general: a derivative cannot have a jump discontinuity.

    At a point where the one-sided limits exist but differ, Darboux forces the derivative to take the values strictly between them — which a step function never does.

    A derivative's discontinuities can only be essential oscillation, like the −cos⁡(1/x)-\cos(1/x)−cos(1/x) of problem 2.
